title: B2B integration modernization is never “one and done”
summary: Explore five B2B integration modernization lessons on automation, platform consolidation, ERP transformation, and AI readiness.
body_markdown:
Your next technology transformation could hinge on the integrations no one remembers until something stops working. An ERP upgrade, cloud migration, acquisition, or AI initiative can expose the integrations that keep partners connected and business processes running.


That became clear to me at OpenText World 2026 in Orlando, where I hosted sessions with two global enterprises at very different points in their B2B integration modernization journeys. One focused on modernizing order-to-cash integration. The other explored a broader shift from legacy integration toward an enterprise platform strategy.


The two companies work in different industries and started from different places, but I took away a lot of the same lessons from both: B2B integration modernization works best when organizations stop treating it as a one-time migration and start building for continuous change.


## **What is B2B integration modernization?**


B2B integration modernization means evolving how applications, ERP systems, trading partners, processes and data connect and work together to[orchestrate business processes](https://blogs.opentext.com/from-integration-to-orchestration-ai-and-the-rise-of-connected-supply-chain/) , while reducing dependence on fragmented or tightly coupled legacy environments. That can involve EDI modernization, ERP integration, APIs, managed file transfer (MFT), platform consolidation, and automation.


Just as importantly, it does not mean throwing everything away and starting over. Good modernization protects what works while making the underlying architecture simpler and easier to change.


The two real-world journeys I encountered at OpenText World presented good examples of what that looks like.


## **Automate order-to-cash at scale**


The first journey comes from a leading enterprise software company with a complex order-to-cash environment.


Its earlier environment relied heavily on manual invoicing and validation, including complex orders with as many as 1,000 lines. Through its work with OpenText, that environment evolved into an automated B2B ecosystem supporting $3.75 billion in annual volume, with 80 to 85% of B2B orders fully automated.


As impressive as these metrics are, the more important part of this story is that the modernized environment also gives teams clearer visibility into order data, allows operations staff to focus on more strategic work, and has helped build trust and improve collaboration across Finance and Operations.


[Lesson 1: Automate the work, not the complexity Counting automated transactions or migrated systems is one way to measure modernization, but the better question is what changed for the business because of that automation: less routine work, better visibility, and more trust and collaboration.](https://www.opentext.com/products/supply-chain-automation)


## **Prepare integration for the next ERP**


Now that same high-tech company is building on that automation as it prepares for an[ERP upgrade](https://blogs.opentext.com/5-integration-moves-that-make-or-break-your-erp-upgrade/) . It plans to further separate the ERP from its partner ecosystem by moving more validation and orchestration into specialized middleware and adopting more API- and JSON-based integration patterns. The goal is to keep any internal changes from disrupting trading partners as much as possible.


[Lesson 2: Don’t rebuild yesterday’s complexity on tomorrow’s ERP An ERP transformation is an opportunity to rethink the integration architecture around it. Miss that opportunity, and an organization can invest significant resources in a new ERP, only to reconnect every old dependency exactly where it was before. Modernization should make the next transformation easier, not simply move today’s complexity somewhere newer.](https://www.opentext.com/solutions/erp-integration-and-transformation)


### **Bring EDI and MFT into a broader integration strategy**


The second journey comes from a leading global oil and gas company with a long history of B2B integration. Over time, its integration strategy has evolved beyond established EDI services toward a broader enterprise integration approach.[Managed file transfer (MFT)](https://www.opentext.com/solutions/managed-file-transfer) offers a useful example. Rather than treating MFT and EDI as separate technology stacks, the company brought these capabilities into its broader[OpenText™ Trading Grid](https://www.opentext.com/products/trading-grid) strategy.


What stood out most was not the consolidation itself, but how the transition protected its existing business ecosystem.


[Lesson 3: Judge modernization by what your partners don’t notice With an extensive community already exchanging business information through its existing environment, the company made continuity a priority. The company wanted to ensure trading partners would not have to navigate major changes. Its priority was simple: Partners should not have to care about the technology changing behind the scenes. They care whether purchase orders arrive and files transfer reliably.](https://www.opentext.com/products/secure-collaboration)


### **Consolidate after M&A without creating another silo**


The oil and gas journey also illustrates a challenge that years of business and technology change often make worse. EDI, APIs, MFT and other integration capabilities tend to develop independently. Add[business restructuring](https://www.opentext.com/solutions/business-restructuring) and the acquisition or divestiture of different business units and point solutions over time, and eventually someone opens the architecture diagram and wonders when it became modern art.


[Lesson 4: Consolidate integration capabilities strategically Companies should ask themselves whether separate integration silos still serve a useful purpose. Bringing complementary B2B capabilities into a broader platform strategy can simplify operations and provide a more consistent foundation for automation and future change.](https://www.opentext.com/products/supply-chain-orchestration)


## **Five principles for B2B integration modernization**


Put the two stories together and five practical principles emerge.


1. **Use business change as a modernization trigger.**
ERP transformation is one catalyst, but cloud migration, M&A, divestitures, and legacy technology retirement can expose the same integration complexity.
2. **Protect business continuity.**
Modernization should not require every trading partner to modernize at the same time.
3. **Decouple where it creates flexibility.**
Separating partner connections, validation, and orchestration from individual applications can make future changes less disruptive.
4. **Consolidate strategically.**
Look across EDI, APIs, MFT, and other integration technologies for unnecessary fragmentation rather than creating a new silo for every requirement.
5. **Automate with an outcome in mind.**
Achieving a high percentage of B2B order automation is impressive, but the bigger story is what automation enables: greater visibility, more strategic use of operations resources, and stronger trust in the process.


## **Where AI fits into B2B integration modernization**


AI readiness adds another reason to modernize the integration foundation. If important business information remains scattered across fragmented applications, integrations and partner ecosystems, adding AI does not magically remove the fragmentation.


With every modernization effort, look for opportunities to strengthen your integration and data foundation, not just for today’s transformation, but for AI readiness and whatever innovation comes next.


## **Seven questions to ask before modernizing**


If your organization is approaching an ERP transformation, cloud migration, or legacy integration replacement, ask:


1. How tightly coupled are our trading partner connections to the ERP?
2. Which manual validation and exception processes could we automate?
3. How many separate technologies support EDI, APIs, MFT, and partner connectivity?
4. Could we replace an internal system with minimal disturbance to our trading partners?
5. Where do business users lack visibility into transactions and exceptions?
6. Which business rules should remain independent of the ERP?
7. Does our integration architecture provide the connected, trusted data needed for future automation and AI?


Together, those answers provide a better picture of modernization readiness than technology age alone.


## **Build for the next transformation**


The lesson I took away from these two conversations at OpenText World is simple:
**The best modernization project doesn’t just solve today’s problem. It makes tomorrow’s change easier.**


There will always be another ERP change, acquisition, partner requirement, cloud initiative, or new technology around the corner. Because if we can confidently predict one thing about the technology roadmap, it is that this will not be your last transformation.
